papers.title: TeleSound-Codec: High-Fidelity General Audio Coding Under 1kbps via Language-Grounded Supervision and Scalable Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: High-fidelity general audio coding at ultra-low bitrates is crucial for applications ranging from low-bandwidth communication to audio-language modeling. However, existing neural audio codecs struggle under extreme bitrate constraints, exhibiting degraded performance: weak semantic alignment leads to semantic distortion, while limited generative capacity compromises acoustic fidelity. To address these challenges, we propose TeleSound?Codec, a scalable general audio codec that preserves semantic integrity and fine acoustic details together via language?grounded supervision and scalable generative modeling. Specifically, to achieve strong semantic alignment, we propose to train a semantic encoder under the guidance of a pre-trained large language model. This language-grounded supervision grounds codec latents in human-interpretable linguistic spaces, enhancing semantic integrity and facilitating downstream applications. To improve generative capacity, we further propose training a flow-matching-based generative decoder jointly with an acoustic encoder that captures residual acoustic details. This scalable generative modeling design enables reconstruction quality to scale with computation. Experiments demonstrate that, when scaling the model size to 1.8B parameters, TeleSound-Codec achieves high-fidelity reconstruction of 32kHz general audio—including speech, music, and other sound types—at bitrates as low as 0.275kbps. We present demos on: https://aisaka0v0.github.io/codec\_demo/.

papers.title: Active Acoustic Probes for AI Voice Call Detection
papers.abstract: AI voice calls are making it increasingly practical to impersonate people during live audio conversations, whether through voice cloning, real-time conversion, or autonomous voice agents. Current defenses remain mostly passive: they inspect received audio for artifacts created by current generators, which locks defenders into an arms race structurally favoring the attacker. Active defenses invert this dynamic by injecting fresh evidence during the call, but they typically require the remote speaker to cooperate by performing a challenge task. We propose an active acoustic probe that requires no such cooperation: it verifies whether the returned audio traversed a genuine physical speaker-to-microphone path. During a call, the verifier sends a brief high-frequency acoustic challenge and checks whether it survives in the returned audio. Normal physical paths preserve the challenge, whereas the tested voice-conversion paths suppress it. This yields a simple, explainable signal-processing rule calibrated only on normal physical-path recordings. The probe is correctly detected in 99% of trials across diverse consumer audio form factors, from open laptop/phone playback to ear-worn headphones and earbuds, while all 200 outputs from four tested speech-to-speech and voice-conversion configurations fail the detector.

papers.title: "It Scams In The Family:" GenAI Voice Cloning Scams among Sighted and Families with Blind or Low Vision Members
papers.abstract: The usual victim in phone scams is an individual at risk of being defrauded or whose identity might be stolen. But a new scamming scheme has emerged, targeting families as victims instead - an individual at risk of being defrauded through an emergency request, voiced by a clone of a related individual whose voice identity has been non-consensually sampled. As these scams are harmful both to the well-being and individuals' true identity (voice), in addition to financial loss, we set to ''conceptually replicate'' an early exploration done by Sharevski et al. (2025) through naturalistically resembling experiences with n1=10 families involving sighted and n2=10 involving a blind or a low vision member (pairs of a 'caller' and 'callee', n=40 total). Our thematic analysis uncovered an overarching attitude of ''self-preparedness'' to withstand these scams, based on both 'intrinsic' motivation to ward off pressure to act on an emotional impulse and 'extrinsic' motivation to avoid immediate and long-term victimization. Expanding the original study's findings with the experiences of a population reliant on voice both as a medium and as an access, we draw on the resilience themes to sketch out 'user-sensitive' accessible designs against GenAI scams.

papers.title: Beyond Known Speakers: Enhancing Spoofing Detection Generalization with VIVED
papers.abstract: Recent speech synthesis systems have moved beyond conventional voice cloning toward the generation of expressive, text-described virtual identities. This shift creates a generalization challenge for spoofing countermeasures trained primarily on cloned speech from a limited pool of reference speakers and relatively neutral read-speech content. We introduce Virtual Identities with Varied Emotional Dynamics (VIVED), a large-scale dataset designed to improve robustness against text-driven virtual voices. VIVED is built around three principles. First, it generates over 100,000 synthetic virtual identities from stochastic natural-language descriptions sampled from a seven-dimensional acoustic and paralinguistic attribute bank, reducing reliance on real speaker reference audio for spoof generation. Second, it combines linguistically and affectively diverse transcripts from LibriSpeech, TIMIT, and the EmoBox English subset to expose synthesis models to phonetic complexity and emotional prosody. Third, it applies a symmetric domain-matching and acoustic laundering pipeline to both bona fide and synthetic utterances, including multi-codec alignment, room impulse response simulation, noise injection, and codec compression, thereby reducing shortcut learning from channel or processing artifacts. Empirical analysis indicates that VIVED covers a speaker representation space with nearly 1.8 times the Vendi Score of the ASVspoof 5 baseline, substantially reducing the risk of identity memorization. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that training on VIVED systematically enhances robustness to text-driven virtual voices while maintaining competitive cross-corpus performance on ASVspoof 5. Multiple baseline architectures achieve substantially lower EER and minDCF on the VIVED evaluation set compared with models trained only on ASVspoof 5.

papers.title: An Interactive Desktop Application for Human Gesture-Controlled Music Generation Using Deep Learning-Based Hand Tracking
papers.abstract: This paper presents an interactive desktop application for human gesture-controlled music generation. The system uses a standard webcam and deep learning-based hand tracking to detect both hands and convert hand features into musical control actions. The application was developed in Python and uses OpenCV, MediaPipe, FluidSynth, MIDI synthesis, and WAV stem playback. It provides three modes. Free Play lets the user control notes and dynamics with hand movement. Song Generation lets the user guide melody, bass, and chords inside a beat-based structure. Stem Control lets the user activate or mute separate audio stems with finger gestures. Deep learning is used for hand tracking, while musical output is produced through rule-based mappings, MIDI synthesis, and prerecorded WAV stem playback. The system was tested with 30 voluntary participants. The average frame rate was 21.81 fps, and the average MediaPipe inference time was 20.80 ms. The average calibration score was 7.93 out of 8 checks. In Stem Control, an average of 4.80 out of five software-defined task criteria were met. The software-defined beat-drop timing condition was met for 16 of the 30 participants. Questionnaire scores were positive, with 4.57 for ease of use, 3.97 for naturalness, and 4.47 for reuse intention. The results show that webcam-based hand tracking can support interactive music control without requiring specialized hardware.

papers.title: A Language-Routed Speech-to-Action Framework for Code-Switched Indic Voice Assistants
papers.abstract: There are 22 Scheduled Languages in India, along with code-switching, and accents in different dialects make voice the most viable medium for many users of digital public services. There have been remarkable strides in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology for Indic languages, but most assessments are still limited to word error rate (WER). Conversely, LLM agents rely on clean input text and thus conceal the compound failure when the spoken and code-switched object is mapped to the Application Programming Interface (API). In this paper, we introduce IndicAgent-ASR, a cascade of acoustic-to-agent system that performs language/code switch detection, routes speech to Indic or English ASR models, canonicalizes multilingual slots, plans for tool call or dependent tool call, runs a safety filter, and generates a spoken response using Indic text-to-speech. We specify the architecture, an end-to-end flowchart, a turn-level algorithm, and an easily reproducible software stack. Published benchmarking results include multilingual and code-switching baselines for MUCS 2021 with WER scores of 30.73% and 32.45%, best-performing accent models with WER ranging from 10.5% to 20.5% in the LAHAJA benchmark, and parameter filling accuracy of 60.6% (English) against 39.2% (Indic) in VoiceAgentBench using the strongest ASR-LLM pipeline, where sequential dependent calls drop to 10.0% and 4.3%. The feasibility prototype of the Hindi/Hinglish and Marathi language features mandi, weather, e-health record, and balance check tools, but denies voice fund transfer and prompt injection tools. The evidence supports keeping a strong Indic ASR front-end in the cascade and treating dependent tools and safety as first-class modules.

papers.title: PodEval: A Multimodal Evaluation Framework for Long-form Podcast Generation
papers.abstract: Recently, an increasing number of multimodal (text and audio) benchmarks have emerged, primarily focusing on evaluating models' understanding capability. However, exploration into assessing generative capabilities remains limited, especially for open-ended long-form content generation. Significant challenges lie in no reference standard answer, no unified evaluation metrics and uncontrollable human judgments. In this work, we take podcast-like audio generation as a starting point and propose PodEval, a comprehensive and well-designed open-source evaluation framework. In this framework: 1) We construct a real-world podcast dataset spanning diverse topics, serving as a reference for human-level creative quality. 2) We introduce a multimodal evaluation strategy and decompose the complex task into three dimensions: text, speech and audio, with different evaluation emphasis on ''Content'' and ''Format''. 3) For each modality, we design corresponding evaluation methods, involving both objective metrics and subjective listening test. We leverage representative podcast generation systems (including open-source, close-source, and human-made) in our experiments. The results offer in-depth analysis and insights into podcast generation, demonstrating the effectiveness of PodEval in evaluating open-ended long-form audio. This project is fully open-source to facilitate public use: https://github.com/yujxx/PodEval.

papers.title: Bat Vocalization Explorer: An Interactive, Leakage-Controlled Tool for Decoding Behavioural Context from Egyptian Fruit Bat Calls
papers.abstract: We present Bat Vocalization Explorer, an interactive system that demonstrates how discrete tokenization and a simple linear probe decode behavioural context from the vocalizations of Egyptian fruit bats ( Rousettus aegyptiacus ). The tool makes a leakage-controlled companion study tangible to a live audience through (i) a leakage-controlled evaluation---context macro-F1 across in-individual versus held-out (cross-individual, cross-session) splits---that exposes how much an in-individual score is inflated, of which only a small part is genuine identity leakage; and (ii) discrete ''situation markers''---a handful of tokens strongly concentrated in the biting context (P>0.85, ≈8× over base rate)---highlighted live as the user browses through real calls. It also reports (iii) a cautionary, reproducible result that a classical mel front-end beats an audio foundation model (BEATs) on this ultrasonic corpus. The system is self-contained (no external data or GPU), runs in a browser, and is genuinely interactive: attendees browse real calls, run a live cross-individual evaluation (a probe re-trained in the browser on bats they choose to hold out), inspect the discrete tokens, and compose and classify their own token sequences. Live demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/rayskarken/bat-vocalization-explorer.

papers.title: Explaining Suspicious Speech Beyond Binary Deepfake Detection: A Five-Module Proposition-Centered Evidence Profile
papers.abstract: Current deepfake detectors answer only one question: whether a recording sounds synthetic. This is insufficient for forensic analysis because replay, compression, degradation, or voice cloning can hide synthetic artifacts or preserve speaker identity. As a result, one authenticity score may be incomplete or misleading. We propose a proposition-centered evidence profile that examines five questions separately: whether the signal is analyzable, whether the speech is synthetic, who the speaker is, whether the recording was replayed, and whether it contains encoding or resynthesis traces. Each module produces a record containing its proposition, observation, validation domain, triggered limitations, and direction of support. A comparison matrix then classifies each record as consistent, conflicting, uninformative, or outside validation for each candidate production scenario (i.e. a complete hypothesis about a voice record), rather than fusing the outputs into one score. Our contribution is the design and empirical stress evaluation of this forensic workflow and reporting format. Studies 1–4 are proposition-specific stress studies showing how identity, replay, and provenance evidence complement synthetic-speech detection; Study 5 is a paired case-level ablation of the complete profile. Across 3,060 trials from 680 recordings, a deepfake-only report retained the true production scenario in its candidate shortlist in 86.6% of trials, but never reduced the shortlist to that scenario alone. The five-module profile achieved 45.7% correct singleton resolution, meaning that exactly one scenario remained and it was the true one; removing any module reduced this rate. Conversely, hard filtering with all thresholded module outputs excluded the true scenario in the remaining 54.3% of trials, showing why the outputs should expose agreements and conflicts rather than be treated as one automatic verdict. These results demonstrate that suspicious recordings should be assessed through multiple independent forensic questions, with agreements and conflicts reported explicitly.

papers.title: Multi-criteria ranking of open automatic speech recognition models under alternative deployment priorities
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) models differ in accuracy, throughput, and parameter count, so choosing a model involves trade-offs. This study ranks 69 license-eligible open ASR model configurations from the July 2026 open ASR leaderboard, which covers eight short-form English test sets. Criterion weights were derived with the fuzzy analytic hierarchy process (fuzzy AHP) under three illustrative scenarios, each prioritizing one criterion: word error rate (WER), inverse real-time factor (RTFx), or parameter count. The models were then ranked with the technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS). NVIDIA Parakeet-TDT-CTC-110M ranked first in the WER-prioritized scenario, and NVIDIA FastConformer-CTC-large ranked first in the other two. The sensitivity analysis tested three further ranking methods (VIKOR, MABAC, and ARAS), classical AHP and entropy weights, stronger dominance ratings, min–max normalization, 171 weight combinations, and alternative WER measures. Across the four ranking methods and three scenarios, the top rank was always held by one of three NVIDIA models: Parakeet-TDT-CTC-110M, FastConformer-CTC-Large, or Conformer-CTC-Small. Classical AHP weights produced nearly identical rankings (Spearman rank correlation of at least 0.998), and Parakeet-TDT-CTC-110M or FastConformer-CTC-Large ranked first in 163 of the 171 TOPSIS weight combinations. However, under the strongest WER priority tested, the more accurate but larger NVIDIA Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2 ranked first in the WER-prioritized scenario, and ARAS favored the smallest models. The rankings are specific to this benchmark rather than validated recommendations for particular sectors, and any model’s suitability must be verified on representative audio and target hardware before deployment. The framework offers a transparent, reproducible way to compare ASR models under different deployment priorities.

papers.title: Reliability-aware tone–segment learning for weakly supervised Southern Min automatic speech recognition
papers.abstract: Southern Min automatic speech recognition (ASR) is challenged by non-verbatim Mandarin subtitles, unreliable pseudo-transcripts, tone-related acoustic variation, and programme-dependent domain shift. We propose the Southern Min Reliability-Bridging Automatic Speech Recognition framework (MinBridge-ASR), organized around two core mechanisms: cross-scale reliability bridging and branch-selective tone–segment learning. The former combines speech-conditioned character-level refinement of weak subtitles with multi-cue utterance-level weighting of pseudo-transcripts while maintaining teacher–student consistency independently. The latter uses controlled pitch interventions to encourage complementary tone-related and segmental representations while restricting programme- and pseudo-speaker-adversarial learning to the segmental pathway. On MinSpeech, MinBridge-ASR achieved character error rates (CERs) of 17.21%, 22.96%, and 20.10% on the official, primary programme-disjoint, and human-verified evaluations, respectively. Across five programme-disjoint splits, it achieved a mean CER of 23.11 ± 0.44%. Direct lexical-tone evaluation showed that the tonal representation outperformed explicit fundamental-frequency (F0) fusion in tone-category and tonal-minimal-pair discrimination despite lower raw pitch recoverability. Progressive ablations and reliability calibration further supported the two core mechanisms. These results demonstrate improved weakly supervised Southern Min ASR under subtitle noise and programme variation.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: automatic speech recognition

papers.title: Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls
papers.abstract: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference. Thus, measuring only human-likeness or testing one voice per system can misjudge which agents listeners would rather talk to.

# StaleyNET checkpoints

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

## At a glance

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpointed runs | 9 |
| Parameters | 7,099,904 for text-only runs; 7,165,440 for the lyrics runs; 42,858,496 for `pq-large` |
| Transformer | width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, context 768 (`pq-large`: width 512, 8 layers, context 1152) |
| Audio tokens | 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries (`pq-large`: 4 band groups × 4 levels = 16 codebooks of 1024 entries) |
| Audio features | 128 mel bands at 24 kHz, FFT 1024, hop 256 |
| Training data | Song Describer Dataset and JamendoLyrics MultiLang |
| License | CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream dataset terms |

## Checkpoints

| Run | Purpose | Parameters | `best` step | `latest` step | Training tracks |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `thor-base` | base text-to-music model | 7,099,904 | 0 | None | 667 |
| `smoke` | pipeline smoke test | 7,099,904 | 0 | 1,500 | 667 |
| `overfit-one-take` | single-take memorisation check | 7,099,904 | 200 | 200 | 1 |
| `vocal-scratch` | vocal-filtered model from scratch | 7,099,904 | 5,500 | 6,000 | 281 |
| `vocal-finetune` | vocal fine-tune | 7,099,904 | 250 | None | 281 |
| `lyrics-orin` | lyrics-conditioned model | 7,165,440 | 3,750 | 4,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor` | lyrics-conditioned model trained on the AGX Thor | 7,165,440 | 4,750 | 8,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor-long` | the same model trained for 20,000 steps | 7,165,440 | 19,750 | 20,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `pq-large` | larger model on the band-group tokenizer (in progress) | 42,858,496 | 7,000 | 7,000 | 742 (75 with lyrics) |

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

# BA · Your Voice. Your Identity.

BA speaks any text in your own voice, from a 10–15 second recording of you: **Egyptian Arabic**, **English**, and **French (beta)**. Every output carries an inaudible watermark. Use only your own voice or a voice whose owner has given you explicit permission.

**Try it:** [the BA Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mahmoudalyosify/BA) (record or upload your voice, tick the consent box, type, listen).

## What BA is, and what it is built from

BA v0.1.0 is two things:

1. **The VoxCPM2 weights, unmodified.** VoxCPM2 is a 2B-parameter, 48 kHz multilingual text-to-speech model by OpenBMB, released under Apache-2.0. The weight and tokenizer files in this repository are byte-for-byte copies of [`openbmb/VoxCPM2`](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2) at commit `7936080b41163874f38610f46f438e2c0757f9fd` (see `NOTICE`). BA v0.1 does **not** fine-tune or otherwise change them.
2. **The BA engine** (`ba_tts`, this repository's wheel), which decides how the model is driven:
   - prepares the reference recording (mono, trimmed to speech, loudness-normalised, the cleanest stretch chosen; noisy, clipped or too-short audio is refused with a clear message);
   - transcribes the reference with Whisper large-v3-turbo when you give no transcript, and clones with the reference *and* its transcript;
   - writes digits, times, prices, percentages and symbols as Egyptian, English or French words, and writes common English loanwords in Egyptian text in Arabic script;
   - splits long text at sentence boundaries, checks every chunk (duration against text length, empty or clipped audio) and regenerates failures with a new seed;
   - loudness-normalises the result and embeds an [AudioSeal](https://huggingface.co/facebook/audioseal) watermark.

VoxCPM2 was chosen in a bake-off of eight voice-cloning systems on Egyptian Arabic (below). Of the systems eligible as a base (permissively licensed weights with documented training data), it was the only one whose Egyptian output a dialect classifier labelled as Egyptian most of the time.

## Quick start

Python 3.10 or newer. A CUDA GPU is strongly recommended (peak GPU memory in our runs: 8.11 GB allocated, 10.99 GB reserved); CPU works but is slow.

```bash
pip install https://huggingface.co/mahmoudalyosify/BA/resolve/main/ba_tts-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
```

```python
import soundfile as sf
from ba_tts import BA, detect_watermark

ba = BA.from_pretrained("mahmoudalyosify/BA")      # downloads the weights (about 5 GB) on first use
voice = ba.create_voice("my_voice.wav", language="arz")   # 10-15 s of YOUR voice; transcript optional

sr, wav = ba.speak("الميعاد اتغير للساعة 7:30، والتذكرة بقت ب 150 جنيه.", voice, language="arz")
sf.write("out.wav", wav, sr)                        # 48 kHz, watermarked

print(detect_watermark(wav, sr))                    # {'watermarked': True, 'score': ..., 'bits_match': ...}
```

`language` is `"arz"` (Egyptian Arabic), `"en"` or `"fr"`. You can pass several recordings (`create_voice(["a.wav", "b.wav"])`), give the transcript yourself (`transcript="..."`), save a voice for later (`voice.save("me.npz")`, `Voice.load("me.npz")`), and set `seed`, `cfg_value` or `inference_timesteps` in `speak`. Text longer than one chunk is split and joined automatically (up to 5,000 characters).

Command line:

```bash
ba-tts --ref my_voice.wav --lang arz --text "أنا رايح الشغل دلوقتي وهرجع على المغرب." --out out.wav
ba-tts --ref my_voice.wav --lang en --text-file speech.txt --out speech.wav --save-voice me.npz
ba-tts --detect out.wav          # is this file a BA output?
```

A language is listed only if the full system passes gate G3 on held-out texts: failure rate at most 5%; intelligibility within a fixed bound; speaker similarity at least 80% of the similarity between two real recordings of the same speaker; and, for Egyptian, a dialect-ID share at least 60% of the share measured on real colloquial Egyptian speech (otherwise it would be listed only as "Arabic").

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Egyptian Arabic | `arz` | listed | 0/130 | CER 0.030 (bound 0.171) | 0.769 (bar 0.696) | 0.889 (bar 0.54) |
| English | `en` | listed | 0/64 | WER 0.003 (bound 0.08) | 0.779 (bar 0.699) | – |

## Measured results

### Evaluation set

- **Reference voices:** 12 speakers from [FLEURS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/fleurs) (CC-BY-4.0): 6 Egyptian (`ar_eg`, 3 male and 3 female), 3 American English, 3 French; clean clips of 8–15 s. They are used for measurement only; neither these clips nor anything cloned from them is published.
- **Texts:** 40 colloquial Egyptian sentences (everyday talk, questions, numbers and dates, long sentences, a diacritised copy of ten), 20 English, 20 French, 6 Arabic–English code-switched sentences, and one passage of about 120 words per language. Some texts were used to tune the engine; **every number below excludes them** (held-out texts only). BA and raw VoxCPM2 are compared on the same texts, voices and seeds.
- **Automatic metrics, each calibrated on real speech:**
  - words: CER (Egyptian) and WER (English, French) from Whisper large-v3 after normalisation. On real speech the same ASR gives CER 0.071 on colloquial Egyptian and WER 0.052 (English) and 0.062 (French) on FLEURS;
  - voice: cosine similarity of ECAPA-TDNN speaker embeddings between the reference and the output. Two different real clips of the same speaker score 0.870 (Egyptian), 0.874 (English), 0.900 (French); clips of different speakers 0.084–0.184;
  - dialect: share of outputs that the [`badrex/mms-300m-arabic-dialect-identifier`](https://huggingface.co/badrex/mms-300m-arabic-dialect-identifier) classifier labels Egyptian. colloquial Egyptian speech: 0.90 (lahgtna test set; the gate's reference) and 0.98 (NileTTS); Egyptians reading Modern Standard Arabic (FLEURS): 0.34;
  - naturalness: DNSMOS P.808 (real speech: 3.515–3.990);
  - failures: empty, cut off, or a duration far outside what the text length implies.

## How it works

```
your recording(s) ──► reference preparation ──► Whisper large-v3-turbo transcript (if none given)
                                 │                               │
                                 └──────► VoxCPM2 prompt cache (reference audio + transcript)
text ──► language normaliser (numbers, symbols, loanwords) ──► sentence chunks
                                                                 │
          VoxCPM2 generation per chunk, fixed voice and seed ◄───┘
                     │
          chunk check (duration vs text length, empty, clipped) ──► retry with a new seed (up to 2)
                     │
          join with pauses ──► loudness normalisation (−20 LUFS) ──► AudioSeal watermark ──► 48 kHz audio
```

The per-language generation settings (guidance 2.0, 10 steps), the chunk length, the reference noise thresholds and the loanword policy were chosen by measurement on the tuning texts. They are recorded in `ba_config.json`, which also pins the revisions of the ASR model and the watermark weights.

## Limitations

- **No native-listener review of BA's outputs yet.** The only listening test so far rated the raw bake-off outputs (one rater, 6 sentences per system; see Listening check). BA's own outputs, with its normaliser and reference transcript, have not been rated by ear. Every quality number on this card is automatic.
- **Automatic metrics have blind spots.** One dialect classifier decides "Egyptian"; it labels Egyptians reading Modern Standard Arabic as Egyptian only 34% of the time, and the six Egyptian reference voices are FLEURS clips of read MSA, not colloquial speech. DNSMOS was trained on English and is a weak judge of Arabic. Similarity is one embedding model (ECAPA).
- **Digits are measured by ASR.** Whisper writes most spoken numbers back as digits, so the digit-sentence CER shows whether the right number was said, not whether it was said the Egyptian way. The normaliser itself is covered by unit tests.
- **Small sets.** 18 digit sentences, 18 code-switched utterances and 2 passages per language; French rests on 3 voices.
- **Cross-language similarity is lower.** An Egyptian voice speaking French reaches similarity 0.696, exactly 80% of the Egyptian same-speaker ceiling (0.870); speaking English, 0.730. Cross-language use was not part of the gate.
- **Code-switching.** Inside Egyptian text, a fixed list of common English loanwords is written in Arabic script and short upper-case acronyms are spelled letter by letter; other Latin words are left as written and may be mispronounced.
- **Speed.** Timings are on an A40. The Space runs on shared ZeroGPU hardware, where speed and queueing differ. CPU-only use is very slow.
- **Reference quality matters.** Noisy, reverberant, clipped or very short recordings are refused or give a weaker likeness.
- **No fine-tune.** BA v0.1 uses the base weights; anything VoxCPM2 cannot say well, BA cannot either.

## Responsible use

- **Consent.** Use only your own voice, or a voice whose owner has given you explicit permission for this use. Do not impersonate anyone, deceive, defraud, harass, or make non-consensual content. These terms are part of the licence.
- **Watermark.** Every BA output carries an inaudible AudioSeal watermark with the 16-bit message "BA". Anyone can check a file: `ba-tts --detect file.wav`, or `detect_watermark(wav, sr)` in Python. Detection survived MP3 at 64 kbit/s and resampling in our tests; it was not tested against deliberate removal attacks. Do not remove or circumvent it, and do not publish audio made with the watermark switched off (`watermark=False` exists for research measurement).
- **The Space.** Generation is blocked until you tick the consent box. Uploads are processed in a per-request temporary directory that is deleted after the request, together with Gradio's own copies; the voice prepared from them lives only in your browser session's memory. Generated audio sits in Gradio's cache only so the player and download work, and is swept every few minutes. No text or audio is logged; flagging and analytics are off. Nothing you upload is used for training.

# MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct for gufo (GGUF: audio encoder BF16 + LLM Q8_0)

## What this is

MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct (music understanding: description, lyrics, structure, questions about a
clip) in the two-file GGUF layout that the native port in
[gufo-studio-windows](https://github.com/D3rPapst/gufo-studio-windows) (`gufo serve moss-music`,
branch `feat/moss-music-21`) loads on AMD Strix Halo under Windows. No Python, no torch.

* `moss-music-8b.audio.gguf` (1.72 GB): Whisper-style audio encoder (Conv2d stem, 32 layers),
  `audio_adapter` and the three DeepStack mergers. Architecture `moss-music`; tensor names are
  the Hugging Face names, matrices BF16, vectors F32.
* `moss-music-8b.llm-Q8_0.gguf` (8.71 GB): the Qwen3-8B language model as a standard
  llama.cpp `qwen3` GGUF, Q8_0 (254 Q8_0 + 145 F32 tensors), tokenizer and chat template
  included.

## Source and licence

* Original: [OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/OpenMOSS-Team/MOSS-Music-8B-Instruct)
  (revision `fce7f830`), OpenMOSS Team with MOSI.AI and the Shanghai Innovation Institute.
* Licence: the model card declares `license: apache-2.0` and states
  "Models in MOSS-Music are licensed under the Apache License 2.0." The repository ships no
  LICENSE file; the Apache License 2.0 text is included here as `LICENSE`.
* Code: [github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Music](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Music).

## How it was converted

1. `tools/moss_music/convert_hf_to_gufo.py all` (gufo-studio-windows, branch `feat/moss-music`,
   commit `a9d7c2b7` and later) streams the four safetensors shards tensor by tensor: it writes
   the audio GGUF and a plain `Qwen3ForCausalLM` folder for the language model
   (`language_model.*` renamed to `model.*`).
2. llama.cpp `convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype bf16`, then `llama-quantize` to Q8_0
   (llama.cpp build b1351). Run on 12 Nov 2026; sizes 1,724,490,048 and 8,709,518,144 bytes.
3. Regression: 5 test clips, 64 greedy tokens, argmax and top-5 recorded in the port's
   `tests/models/moss_music/regression-q8-2026-11-12.json`.

## How to use with gufo

```ini

command = <gufo.exe>
args = serve moss-music
```

1 GB while loading.

# Haru-4B — full-duplex speech in one file, no Python

[Haru-4B](https://huggingface.co/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B) by higurashi-ai listens and speaks at the same time,
like a person on a phone call: every 133 ms it takes one frame of the user's audio and produces one frame of
its own audio and text. This repository packages it as one [CMF](https://github.com/infosave2007/cmf) file
for `cortiq`, a Rust engine with no Python and no ML framework — the Qwen3.5-4B language model, the audio
projectors, the MeanFlow head and the VibeVoice codec together.

- **RTX A5000, CUDA: 23 ms per 133 ms frame** — 5.8× faster than real time. Vulkan 53 ms, Apple M4 (Metal) 84 ms.
- The codec matches the PyTorch reference within 1.3·10⁻³.

**Listen:** [a conversation](https://huggingface.co/infosave/Haru-4B-cmf/resolve/main/samples/conversation_stereo.mp3)
— the user on the left channel, Haru on the right. The user asks *"Hi! How are you doing today? Could you tell me
something interesting about the ocean?"*; Haru, speaking with the
[reference voice](https://huggingface.co/infosave/Haru-4B-cmf/resolve/main/samples/voice_reference.mp3), answers
*"Hey, welcome to our daily talk show… Today I'm gonna be talking about science, but not just any science, the
science of the ocean."* Both input voices were made with cortiq's Qwen3-TTS.

## Quick start

```bash
cargo install cortiq-cli --features cuda   # NVIDIA: the CUDA backend; without the feature: Vulkan, or Metal on a Mac
hf download infosave/Haru-4B-cmf haru-4b-q8_2f.cmf --local-dir .
CMF_GPU=cuda cortiq duplex haru-4b-q8_2f.cmf user.wav reply.wav --reference voice.wav --stereo --transcript reply.jsonl
```

`user.wav` is played to the model frame by frame, exactly as in a live call, and `reply.wav` is what the model
says over the same span (`--stereo`: the user left, the model right). Leave silence after a question so the
model has time to answer. `--reference` sets the voice: 3 s to 3 min of one speaker, clean speech — use only
voices you have the right to use. Other options: `--system-prompt` (a character card, as the Haru repository
describes it), `--speak-first`, `--temperature` (0.7), `--top-k` (25), `--guidance-scale` (1.5), `--seed`.

## File

| file | size | |
|---|---:|---|
| `haru-4b-q8_2f.cmf` | 6.37 GB | the language model in 8-bit (q8_2f), the head and the codec in f16 |

Four-bit weights break this model: with q4tp, even with only the feed-forward layers at four bits, the text
stream turns to noise. There is no smaller file.

## Speed

Per 133 ms frame, after the prompt and the voice reference, which run once (4–13 s):

- **RTX A5000 (24 GB), CUDA:** 23 ms.
- **RTX A5000, Vulkan:** 53 ms.
- **Apple M4 (24 GB), Metal:** 84 ms.

## Notes

Haru-4B is a pretrained base model released for research: it holds a natural conversation, but it is not a
source of facts and does not follow instructions like an assistant. It can imitate the voice of a reference
clip; only use voices you have the right to use. The live, microphone-in-the-loop demo is in the
[Haru repository](https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru); `cortiq duplex` runs the same loop over a recording.

# TTS accent ivoirien (Noushi et Franco-Bété)

Modèle de synthèse vocale expressive (**Text-to-Speech / Clonage Vocal**) basé sur **`coqui/XTTS-v2`**, spécialisé dans le **français ivoirien naturel** (registre **Nouchi** et **Franco-Bété**) avec gestion native d'émotions et de sons paralinguistiques via **12 Special Tokens Atomiques**.

---

## Points forts du modèle

1. **Accent et prosodie authentiques de Côte d'Ivoire (Nouchi & Franco-Bété)** : entraîné sur des enregistrements vocaux WhatsApp réels, transcrits mot à mot à l'oreille pour préserver l'articulation, les expressions ivoiriennes et le timbre naturel des locuteurs.
2. **3 voix distinctes intégrées** (`references_voix/`) :
   - `issouf` — timbre grave, posé ou expressif
   - `isaac` — timbre dynamique et spontané
   - `seitonne` — timbre naturel conversationnel
3. **12 Special Tokens Atomiques injectés dans `vocab.json` (IDs `6668..6679`, `"special": true`)** :
   - **Émotions** : `[joyeux]`, `[amusé]`, `[enthousiaste]`, `[étonné]`, `[sérieux]`, `[calme]`, `[neutre]`
   - **Balises paralinguistiques** : `<rire>`, `<gloussement>`, `<soupir>`, `<inspiration>`, `<exclamation>`
   *(Chaque balise est encodée en 1 token atomique unique — elle n'est jamais lue syllabe par syllabe comme un mot français.)*
4. **Conditionnement timbre naturel** : utilise 2 prises studio pures par voix avec `sound_norm_refs=False` afin de conserver 100 % du grain vocal original sans déformation spectrale ni souffle parasite.

---

## Structure du dépôt

```text
.
├── README.md
├── inferer_tts_ivoirien.py        # Script d'inférence prêt à l'emploi
├── config.json                     # Configuration XTTS-v2
├── vocab.json                      # Tokenizer BPE + 12 Special Tokens Atomiques (6668..6679)
├── model.pth                       # Poids fine-tunés XTTS-v2
├── dvae.pth                        # Encodeur/Décodeur acoustique DVAE
├── mel_stats.pth                   # Statistiques Mel
├── metadata/
│   └── banque_references_emotions.json
└── references_voix/
    ├── issouf_ref_1.wav
    ├── issouf_ref_2.wav
    ├── isaac_ref_1.wav
    ├── isaac_ref_2.wav
    ├── seitonne_ref_1.wav
    └── seitonne_ref_2.wav
```

---

## Installation

```bash
pip install -U "coqui-tts" "huggingface_hub>=0.27.0" "soundfile" "numpy>=2.0.0,<2.3.0"
pip install --no-deps torchaudio
```

> **Note de compatibilité PyTorch 2.6+ & NumPy 2.x** :  
> Coqui `XTTS-v2` passe parfois `weights_only=True` lors du chargement des checkpoints (`XttsConfig` / `XttsAudioConfig`), ce qui est bloqué par PyTorch 2.6+. Le script d'inférence ci-dessous inclut le correctif propre `weights_only=False` ainsi que la compatibilité `np.long` pour SciPy/Transformers.

---

## Code d'inférence complet (Python)

Enregistrez le script [inferer_tts_ivoirien.py](./inferer_tts_ivoirien.py) ou exécutez directement l'exemple ci-dessous :

```python
import os
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import soundfile as sf
import torch
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

# Compatibilité NumPy >= 2.0 / SciPy et PyTorch >= 2.6 avec les checkpoints Coqui XTTS-v2
if not hasattr(np, "long"):
    np.long = np.int_

_torch_load_origine = torch.load


def _torch_load_compat(*args, **kwargs):
    kwargs["weights_only"] = False
    return _torch_load_origine(*args, **kwargs)


torch.load = _torch_load_compat

from TTS.tts.configs.xtts_config import XttsConfig
from TTS.tts.models.xtts import Xtts

ID_DEPOT_HF = "Tree-AI-lab/tts-accent-ivoirien-noushi-franco-bete"
EMOTIONS_VALIDES = {
    "joyeux",
    "amusé",
    "enthousiaste",
    "étonné",
    "sérieux",
    "calme",
    "neutre",
}
LOCUTEURS_DISPONIBLES = ("issouf", "isaac", "seitonne")


class SynthetiseurTtsIvoirien:
    """Chargeur et moteur d'inférence pour TTS accent ivoirien (Noushi et Franco-Bété)."""

    def __init__(self, dossier_modele: Path, peripherique: str | None = None) -> None:
        self.dossier_modele = dossier_modele
        self.peripherique = peripherique or ("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
        self.etat = "chargement"
        self.modele = None

        fichiers_requis = ["config.json", "vocab.json", "model.pth"]
        for nom in fichiers_requis:
            chemin = self.dossier_modele / nom
            if not chemin.exists():
                self.etat = "erreur"
                raise FileNotFoundError(f"Fichier modèle introuvable : {chemin}")

        try:
            config = XttsConfig()
            config.load_json(str(self.dossier_modele / "config.json"))
            self.modele = Xtts.init_from_config(config)
            self.modele.load_checkpoint(
                config,
                checkpoint_dir=str(self.dossier_modele),
                checkpoint_path=str(self.dossier_modele / "model.pth"),
                vocab_path=str(self.dossier_modele / "vocab.json"),
                eval=True,
                use_deepspeed=False,
            )
            self.modele.to(self.peripherique)
            self.etat = "pret"
        except Exception as err:
            self.etat = "erreur"
            raise RuntimeError(f"Échec du chargement du modèle XTTS-v2 : {err}") from err

    def recuperer_references_voix(self, locuteur: str, emotion: str = "enthousiaste") -> list[str]:
        if locuteur not in LOCUTEURS_DISPONIBLES:
            raise ValueError(f"Locuteur inconnu '{locuteur}'. Choix : {LOCUTEURS_DISPONIBLES}")

        dossier_refs = self.dossier_modele / "references_voix"
        refs_emo = sorted(str(p) for p in dossier_refs.glob(f"{locuteur}_{emotion}_ref_*.wav"))[:2]
        if refs_emo:
            return refs_emo

        refs = sorted(str(p) for p in dossier_refs.glob(f"{locuteur}_ref_*.wav"))[:2]
        if not refs:
            raise FileNotFoundError(
                f"Aucune référence audio trouvée pour '{locuteur}' dans {dossier_refs}."
            )
        return refs

    def synthetiser(
        self,
        texte: str,
        locuteur: str = "issouf",
        emotion: str = "enthousiaste",
        chemin_sortie: str | Path = "sortie_ivoirienne.wav",
        temperature: float = 0.70,
        repetition_penalty: float = 2.5,
    ) -> Path:
        texte_propre = " ".join(texte.split()).strip()
        if not texte_propre:
            raise ValueError("Le texte à synthétiser est vide.")
        if emotion not in EMOTIONS_VALIDES:
            raise ValueError(f"Émotion '{emotion}' invalide. Choix : {sorted(EMOTIONS_VALIDES)}")

        # Ajoute la balise émotionnelle en préfixe si elle n'est pas déjà présente
        if not texte_propre.startswith("["):
            texte_final = f"[{emotion}] {texte_propre}"
        else:
            texte_final = texte_propre

        refs_audio = self.recuperer_references_voix(locuteur, emotion=emotion)

        # Conditionnement timbre naturel (sans écrasement spectral sound_norm_refs)
        latent_cond, emb_locuteur = self.modele.get_conditioning_latents(
            audio_path=refs_audio,
            gpt_cond_len=30,
            gpt_cond_chunk_len=4,
            max_ref_length=30,
            sound_norm_refs=False,
        )

        resultat = self.modele.inference(
            text=texte_final,
            language="fr",
            gpt_cond_latent=latent_cond,
            speaker_embedding=emb_locuteur,
            temperature=temperature,
            length_penalty=1.0,
            repetition_penalty=repetition_penalty,
            top_k=50,
            top_p=0.85,
            enable_text_splitting=True,
        )

        cible = Path(chemin_sortie)
        cible.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        sf.write(str(cible), resultat["wav"], 24000)
        return cible
```

```bash
python inferer_tts_ivoirien.py \
  --locuteur issouf \
```

```bash
python inferer_tts_ivoirien.py \
  --locuteur isaac \

  --sortie audio_soupir.wav
```
